title: Making a New World: Founding Capitalism in the Bajío
author: John Tutino
tl: China decreta plata como única moneda mundial

A new world began in the 1550s when the emperor of Ming China declared silver the only money for trade and taxation. Half a world away mines at Taxco and Pachuca, at Guanajuato and Zacatecas turned to make silver to meet rising Chinese demand.
p. xiv
Dos Bajíos: pueblo otomí y plata global

Around 1600, New Spain solidified a dynamic silver economy set in two distinct regional ways of making maize. In the heartland, natives kept land in self-governing republics. In the Bajío, Mesoamerican migrants became resident laborers on estates.
p. xviii
Revueltas populares contra las reformas borbónicas

Chapter 2 turns to the imperial challenges, silver dynamism, and population pressures that merged to generate the predations that would drive the risings of 1810. It examines the imperial impositions that led to local riots at Guanajuato in 1766 and 1767.
Hambruna del año del hambre en el Bajío

It follows the revival of silver in the 1770s and the challenges of sustenance that came with the deadly drought and famine of 1785 and 1786. It focuses on the predations imposed on estate communities after 1790 as silver drove to new peaks.
Las muchachas ocupan Puerto de Nieto

In 1802, 'las muchachas'—the girls—occupied the home of manager don José Antonio Rico at Puerto de Nieto, a large landed estate set between the mining center of Guanajuato and Querétaro, the Americas' leading textile city, in the rich basin known as the Bajío.
p. xiii
Napoleón captura a los Borbones y quiebra la soberanía

Saint-Domingue and its revenues lost, in May 1808 Napoleon invaded Spain, aiming to claim the silver flows still rising in New Spain. He captured Madrid and its Bourbon monarchs, breaking Spain's imperial regime. He failed to gain New Spain's silver.
Cae Epigmenio González en Querétaro

He joined debates in the summer of 1810 led by corregidor don Miguel Domínguez; councilman, merchant, and landlord don Pedro de Septién; and Hidalgo, too. While they talked, González wrote a plan to force estates to lease lands to family growers.
Grito de Dolores

Hidalgo called his parishioners at Dolores took arms on September 16. He demanded political rights, to see thousands of men raise machetes to assault landed power. Leaders demanding political autonomy defended property while hungry insurgents sacked estates.
El Pípila incendia la Alhóndiga de Granaditas

Together they invaded the mining city of Guanajuato: Hidalgo claiming silver to fund his fight; popular rebels, rural and urban, taking maize to feed insurgents. Hidalgo's rebels sacked Guanajuato, taking silver and maize in the siege of the Alhóndiga.
p. xiii–13
Insurgencia popular regresa a la tierra

When Hidalgo faced political defeat early in 1811, rebels from Puerto de Nieto and estates all around Guanajuato returned home to press a decade of popular insurgency, taking estate lands to make maize to feed families and guerrilla bands.
p. xiv
Derrota de Puente de Calderón

Rebels retreated to sack Guanajuato again, then assembled west around Guadalajara. As Hidalgo refused popular demands for redistribution, the revolt broke at Puente de Calderón early in 1811. The rising shook viceregal power. Revolution had just begun.
La plata novohispana cae a la mitad

Mining collapsed, cutting New Spain's silver flows in half by 1812—a devastating 30 percent fall of the global money supply. Historic trades in fine Indian cottons and Chinese silks broke. Silver capitalism broke by 1812; agrarian capitalism dissolved.
p. xiv–13
Morelos y Oviedo: el frente del sur

Don José Sánchez Espinosa backed don Juan Nepomuceno Oviedo, manager of his grazing estates north of the Bajío, to fight Hidalgo and then chase José María Morelos—until Oviedo gave his life blocking the political rebel's route to the capital in 1812.
Expedición liberal de Xavier Mina
They fought through 1817, when Spanish liberal Francisco Javier Mina invaded with a gang of US freebooters declaring liberty, seeking silver, and disrupting insurgency and counterinsurgency.
Pacificación: tierras para las familias campesinas

In 1818, regime forces turned to pacifying amnesties that granted insurgents rights to cultivate estate lands as tenants and keep arms to defend their gains. Commercial cropping gone, tenants paid rents to plant maize while women remained leading growers.
Consumación de la Independencia: 200 años

Royalist commander don Agustin de Iturbide, famous for defeating Morelos and brutalizing popular insurgents across the Bajío, allied with Vicente Guerrero in the Iguala rising that broke with Spain and proclaimed a Mexican empire in 1821.
Banco de Avío y nuevo capitalismo silver-industrial

New industries also began in the 1830s, promoted by Lucas Alamán and the Banco de Avío, the world's first development bank. Cayetano Rubio took capital from trade in silver to build Hércules at Querétaro, a great cotton mill drawing women to its machines.
Invasión estadounidense de 1846

Mining, industry, and family growers thrived during the war provoked by the United States in 1846. Invading armies never neared the basin as national authorities took refuge at Querétaro to gain revenues in Mexico's richest region.
Invasión francesa golpea el Bajío

Mexican conservatives invited Napoleon III to mount the invasion that brought Maximilian of Hapsburg to an imagined Mexican Empire from 1864 to 1867. They pressed battles to take Guanajuato during 1864 and 1865, breaking the dynamism of silver.
Cruz de oro: Estados Unidos abandona la plata

Then, in 1873, the United States—funded by gold mined in lands taken from Mexico—joined England and Germany on a gold standard. Radically devaluing silver, the leading industrial powers ended Mexico's capital independence.
Second revolution: Zapata and land for maize

Heartland communities faced corrosions of autonomies as populations grew while liberal powers privatized their lands. They joined Emiliano Zapata to drive a second revolution in 1910, gaining land to sustain families and a new national industrial capitalism.
p. xxi
